# Additional Resources: Nature of Financial Risk

The readings below extend the foundations covered in this subtopic. Each is a primary or authoritative source already drawn on in the Course Content, so working through them deepens your grasp of the definitions, distinctions, and the Lehman illustration rather than introducing unrelated material. A suggested study order follows the list to match the flow of the lesson.

## Foundational Concept

### Frank H. Knight, *Risk, Uncertainty, and Profit* (1921)
- Link: https://www.econlib.org/library/Knight/knRUP.html

This is the original source of the risk-versus-uncertainty distinction at the heart of the subtopic. Knight separates uncertainty that can be measured or assigned probabilities ("risk") from deeper uncertainty that cannot be reduced to reliable probabilities. Read the relevant passage to understand why quantitative tools such as value-at-risk and stress testing operate only inside the measurable zone, and why judgment remains essential beyond it. The online edition reproduces the public-domain 1921 text; focus on Part I, Chapter I, where the distinction is developed.

## Core Risk Categories (Supervisory Guidance)

### Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for the Management of Credit Risk*
- Link: https://www.bis.org/publ/bcbs75.htm

Use this to reinforce the credit-risk definition and, crucially, to see how counterparty exposure extends well beyond ordinary loans into bonds, derivatives, guarantees, and settlement activity. It also previews layered risk by noting that settlement risk can combine credit, liquidity, market, operational, and reputational elements.

### Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision*
- Link: https://www.bis.org/publ/bcbs144.htm

This source frames liquidity as the ability to fund assets and meet obligations as they come due without unacceptable losses. It explains why a bank that looks solvent on paper can still fail when funding evaporates, and it connects directly to the contingency-funding and stress-testing themes that recur later in the module.

### Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, market-risk and operational-risk frameworks
- Link: https://www.bis.org/bcbs/publ/d457.htm

This material supports the two remaining core categories. It defines market risk in terms of changes in market factors affecting positions, distinguishes trading-book from banking-book exposures, and introduces expected shortfall and non-modellable risk factors. The companion operational-risk definition explains why operational risk is treated as a distinct category arising from failed processes, people, systems, or external events.

## Layered Risk in Practice

### Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission, *The Financial Crisis Inquiry Report* (2011)
- Link: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GPO-FCIC/pdf/GPO-FCIC.pdf

This official report is the grounding source for the Lehman Brothers case. It documents the firm's reliance on short-term repo funding, its illiquid mortgage-related exposures, the leverage and disclosure concerns around "Repo 105," and the supervisory warnings about risk-management failings. Reading the Lehman sections shows in concrete detail how market, liquidity, solvency, and governance pressures reinforced one another.

## Looking Ahead (Optional Extension)

### Elspeth Wales, "Rise of the chief risk officer," *The CFO* (2002)
- Link: https://the-cfo.io/2002/04/22/rise-of-the-chief-risk-officer/

This trade-press article is an optional bridge to later governance subtopics. It describes how the chief-risk-officer role emerged to give institutions a holistic, integrated view across credit, market, and operational risk rather than managing them in silos. It is most useful once you appreciate why the categories introduced here interact.

## Suggested Study Order

1. Start with Knight to fix the risk-versus-uncertainty foundation.
2. Move through the three Basel sources to anchor the four core categories.
3. Read the Lehman sections of the Financial Crisis Inquiry Report to see the categories interact.
4. Finish with the chief-risk-officer article only if you want an early look at institution-wide oversight covered in later subtopics.
